title: 22 — Testing & Quality
html:
22 — Testing & Quality

The purpose of a test suite is not to find bugs — it's to let you change code with confidence. Every decision below is judged against that: does this test make change safer, or does it make change harder?

1. The shape of a test suite

        Traditional pyramid                    The "testing trophy" (Kent C. Dodds)
              /\   E2E (few)                        ▲  E2E (few)
             /  \                                ████████  Integration (most value)
            /____\  Integration                  ██████████████
           /      \                              ████  Unit
          /________\  Unit (many)                ██  Static (types, lint)

Both are right for different systems. The real question is: where does the risk live?

  • Complex domain logic → more unit tests.
  • Lots of integration between components/services → more integration tests.
  • A thin CRUD layer over a database → integration tests catch far more than unit tests of mappers.

The trophy's underrated insight: static analysis (strict types, nullable reference types, linting) is a test layer, and it's the cheapest one — it runs in your editor and catches whole categories of bug at zero marginal cost.

Anti-pattern — the ice cream cone: many slow, flaky E2E tests, few unit tests. Slow feedback, unreliable signal, and nobody can tell whether a red build is a real failure.

Level Scope Speed Use for
Static Compiler, linter, analyzers Instant Types, nullability, style, known anti-patterns
Unit One class/function, no I/O ms Business logic, algorithms, edge cases, error paths
Integration Several components + real infra 100 ms–s Persistence, HTTP pipeline, serialisation, transactions, SQL
Contract Between two services s API compatibility across teams
E2E The whole system through the UI 10s of s A handful of critical user journeys
Non-functional Load, security, accessibility, chaos minutes Scheduled or gated, not on every PR

2. What makes a good test

F.I.R.S.T. — Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely.

Property Meaning Violation
Fast The suite runs while you wait 30-minute unit tests → nobody runs them locally
Independent Any order, any subset, in parallel Shared static state, database rows left behind, test A seeding test B
Repeatable Same result every run, everywhere DateTime.Now, Random, real network, timezone dependence
Self-validating Pass/fail, no human interpretation Tests that print output for you to eyeball
Timely Written with (or before) the code Retrofitted tests document bugs as features

Test names describe behaviour, not implementation:

// ❌ TestCalculate1, Test_Method_Works, ShouldReturnTrue
// ✔ Method_Scenario_ExpectedOutcome
[Fact] public void AddHolding_WhenTotalWeightWouldExceed100Percent_ThrowsDomainException()
[Fact] public void Calculate_WithEmptyPortfolio_ReturnsZeroOverlap()
[Fact] public void Approve_WhenApproverIsTheCreator_IsRejectedForFourEyesRule()

The name should let you understand a CI failure without opening the test.

Arrange / Act / Assert, with one behaviour per test:

[Fact]
public void AddHolding_WhenTotalWeightWouldExceed100Percent_ThrowsDomainException()
{
    // Arrange
    var portfolio = new Portfolio(PortfolioId.New());
    portfolio.AddHolding(InstrumentId.Parse("AAPL"), new Weight(0.7m));

    // Act
    var act = () => portfolio.AddHolding(InstrumentId.Parse("MSFT"), new Weight(0.4m));

    // Assert
    act.Should().Throw<DomainException>()
       .WithMessage("*exceeding 100%*");
}

⚠️ Test behaviour, not implementation. A test that asserts _repository.Received(1).SaveAsync(...) breaks when you legitimately refactor to batch the save — it tests how, not what. Assert on outcomes and observable state wherever you can.

No logic in tests. If a test contains an if, a loop, or arithmetic that recomputes the expected value, it can be wrong in the same way the code is wrong. Use parameterised tests with literal expected values.

[Theory]
[InlineData(100.00, 3, 33.34, 33.33, 33.33)]   // remainder to the first participant
[InlineData(10.00,  4, 2.50,  2.50,  2.50)]
public void SplitEqually_DistributesRemainderDeterministically(
    decimal total, int people, params decimal[] expected) { ... }

3. Test doubles

Double Behaviour Use
Dummy Passed but never used Filling a required parameter
Stub Returns canned answers Providing input to the code under test
Fake A working, simplified implementation In-memory repository, fake clock. Often the best option
Spy Records how it was called Verifying a notification was sent
Mock Pre-programmed with expectations, verifies interactions Genuine interaction contracts

Guidelines:

  1. Mock what you own. Wrap third-party SDKs in your own interface and mock that; mocking a vendor type couples your tests to their design and lets their behaviour change silently.
  2. Don't mock value objects or DTOs. Just construct them.
  3. Prefer fakes to mocks for anything used in many tests — a fake repository stays readable where twenty Returns(...) setups don't.
  4. ⚠️ Over-mocking produces tests that pass while the system is broken. If every collaborator is mocked, you've tested that your code calls the methods you told it to call.
  5. Don't mock the database. Use a real one via Testcontainers (§5).
// A fake is often clearer and more reusable than repeated mock setup
public sealed class InMemoryPortfolioRepository : IPortfolioRepository
{
    private readonly Dictionary<PortfolioId, Portfolio> _store = [];
    public Task<Portfolio?> GetAsync(PortfolioId id, CancellationToken ct) =>
        Task.FromResult(_store.GetValueOrDefault(id));
    public Task SaveAsync(Portfolio p, CancellationToken ct) { _store[p.Id] = p; return Task.CompletedTask; }
}

Time, randomness, and IDs must be injected or your tests are non-deterministic:

var clock = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 7, 27, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
var sut = new SettlementService(repository, clock);
clock.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(3));      // deterministic time travel, no Thread.Sleep

4. TDD — the parts that are actually useful

flowchart LR
    R["🔴 RED<br/>write a failing test<br/>for the next behaviour"] --> G["🟢 GREEN<br/>simplest code<br/>that passes"]
    G --> RF["🔵 REFACTOR<br/>improve structure,<br/>tests stay green"]
    RF --> R

What TDD genuinely gives you: a design forced to be testable (which usually means well-decoupled), a guaranteed-executable specification, no untested code, and — the most underrated part — a test you have seen fail, so you know it can fail.

Where it fits well: algorithms, business rules, bug fixes (write the failing regression test first — this is non-negotiable), parsers, calculations, anything with clear inputs and outputs. Where it fits badly: exploratory/spike work, UI layout, integration glue, and situations where you don't yet know the desired interface. Writing the code first and the tests immediately after is a legitimate practice — "tests eventually" is not.

The bug-fix discipline (apply it always):

  1. Reproduce the bug with a failing test.
  2. Confirm the test fails for the right reason.
  3. Fix.
  4. Test passes.
  5. Keep the test forever — it's now a permanent regression guard.

5. Integration testing

// A real SQL Server, per test run, via Docker — no in-memory substitutes
public sealed class DatabaseFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MsSqlContainer _container = new MsSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest")
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => _container.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _container.StartAsync();
        await MigrationRunner.ApplyAsync(ConnectionString);   // the REAL migrations
    }

    public Task DisposeAsync() => _container.DisposeAsync().AsTask();
}

public sealed class TradeRepositoryTests(DatabaseFixture fixture) : IClassFixture<DatabaseFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Save_WhenDuplicateTradeReference_ViolatesUniqueConstraint()
    {
        await using var connection = new SqlConnection(fixture.ConnectionString);
        var repository = new TradeRepository(connection);
        await repository.SaveAsync(TradeFactory.Create(reference: "TR-001"), default);

        var act = () => repository.SaveAsync(TradeFactory.Create(reference: "TR-001"), default);

        await act.Should().ThrowAsync<SqlException>().Where(e => e.Number == 2627);
    }
}

⚠️ Never use EF Core's UseInMemoryDatabase for tests that matter. It doesn't enforce constraints, doesn't run SQL, has different transaction semantics, and supports LINQ that your real provider can't translate. Tests pass; production fails. Use Testcontainers, or SQLite only when you've accepted its differences.

Isolation between integration tests — pick one and be consistent:

Strategy Speed Isolation
Transaction rollback per test Fastest Good, but breaks if the code under test manages its own transactions
Respawn/truncate between tests Fast Full
Fresh database per test class Slow Complete
Unique data per test (prefix keys) Fast Partial — accumulates data

API-level integration tests exercise the real middleware pipeline:

public sealed class ApiTests(CustomWebApplicationFactory factory)
    : IClassFixture<CustomWebApplicationFactory>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task PostTrade_WithNegativeNotional_Returns422WithProblemDetails()
    {
        var client = factory.CreateAuthenticatedClient(role: "Trader");
        var response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/api/v1/trades",
            new { instrumentCode = "AAPL", notional = -100m, currency = "GBP" });

        response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.UnprocessableEntity);
        var problem = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<ProblemDetails>();
        problem!.Extensions.Should().ContainKey("errors");
    }
}

External HTTP dependencies: use WireMock.Net to stub the wire, not a mock of your client class — that way you also test your serialisation, headers, timeouts, and error mapping.

6. E2E testing

Keep it to the handful of journeys where failure is unacceptable: log in, the primary workflow, checkout/submit, and one critical report. Ten reliable E2E tests beat two hundred flaky ones.

// Playwright — resilient selectors, no arbitrary waits
test('analyst can run an overlap report', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/portfolios');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Global Equity Fund' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Run overlap' }).click();

  // Auto-waiting on the assertion — never page.waitForTimeout()
  await expect(page.getByTestId('overlap-result')).toContainText('%');
  await expect(page.getByRole('table')).toBeVisible();
});

Rules for stable E2E:

  • Never sleep. Wait on a condition (element visible, network idle, response received).
  • Semantic selectors (getByRole, getByLabel) or explicit data-testid — never CSS classes or DOM paths.
  • Each test creates its own data via API/seed, and cleans up. Shared fixtures create order dependence.
  • Run against a production-shaped environment, in CI, on every merge.
  • Quarantine flaky tests immediately — a suite people don't trust is worse than no suite, because red builds stop meaning anything. Fix or delete within a sprint.

7. Beyond example-based tests

7.1 Property-based testing

Instead of specific examples, assert invariants over generated inputs; the framework finds counterexamples and shrinks them to the minimal failing case.

[Property]
public Property SplitEqually_AlwaysSumsToTheTotal(PositiveInt pennies, PositiveInt people)
{
    var total  = Money.FromMinorUnits(pennies.Get, Currency.Gbp);
    var shares = new EqualSplit().Split(total, Participants(people.Get));
    return (shares.Sum(s => s.Amount.ToMinorUnits()) == pennies.Get)
        .ToProperty();
}

Great for: round-trip properties (serialise→deserialise==original), invariants (sums, ordering, idempotence), commutativity, parsers, and anything with arithmetic. It finds the edge cases you'd never think to write.

7.2 Mutation testing

Deliberately introduces small changes (> → >=, + → -, remove a statement) and checks whether any test fails. A surviving mutant means that line is not really covered by an assertion. This is the honest answer to "is our coverage meaningful?" — coverage says a line executed; mutation testing says a behaviour is actually asserted. Run it periodically on critical modules (Stryker.NET), not on every PR (it's slow).

7.3 Contract testing

Prevents "we changed the API and broke a consumer we didn't know about". Provider verifies against consumer-published expectations in CI (Pact), or an OpenAPI/schema diff fails the build on a breaking change. Essential once more than one team consumes your API or events. See files 14 §8 and 15 §8.

7.4 Snapshot / approval testing

Capture a complex output (generated file, report, HTML) once, review it, commit it, and fail on unexpected diffs. ⚠️ Only useful with disciplined review of the diff — blindly re-approving snapshots is worse than having no test.

8. Coverage — use it correctly

Coverage measures what was executed, not what was verified. A test with no assertions gives 100% coverage.

Metric What it tells you
Line Which lines ran
Branch Which decision outcomes ran — more useful than line
Mutation Which behaviours are actually asserted — the real measure

Sane targets: 80%+ on domain/business logic; lower on infrastructure and generated code. Do not set a blanket organisational target and gate on it — it produces assertion-free tests written to satisfy the number.

The useful gate: coverage must not decrease on changed lines. It focuses attention on new code without incentivising theatre on legacy code.

Track what's uncovered rather than the percentage. An uncovered catch block in a payment path matters; an uncovered ToString() override does not.

9. CI quality gates

flowchart LR
    A[Push / PR] --> B["Static: build with warnings-as-errors,<br/>format, analyzers, lint"]
    B --> C["Unit tests + coverage delta"]
    C --> D["Security: SAST, secret scan, SCA"]
    D --> E["Integration tests (Testcontainers)"]
    E --> F["Contract / API diff"]
    F --> G["Build + publish artifact"]
    G --> H["Deploy to test env"]
    H --> I["E2E smoke + accessibility"]
    I --> J[Promote]

Gate design principles: fail fast (cheapest checks first); PR feedback under ~10 minutes or people stop reading it; no flaky test is allowed to remain in the blocking path; nightly jobs for the slow suites (full E2E, mutation, load, full dependency audit); and the pipeline must be re-runnable without side effects.

Definition of done for a change:

  • Code + tests written and passing locally
  • New logic covered; bug fix has a regression test that fails without the fix
  • Static analysis and security scans clean
  • Documentation/ADR updated if behaviour or design changed
  • Observability added for new critical paths (logs, metrics, traces)
  • Reviewed and approved
  • Deployable and reversible (feature-flagged if risky)

10. Non-functional testing

Type Question Tool
Load Does it meet the SLO at expected volume? k6, NBomber, JMeter
Stress Where does it break, and how? Same, ramped past capacity
Soak Does it survive 24 hours? (leaks, connection exhaustion) Same, sustained
Spike Does it survive 10× in 30 seconds? Same
Security OWASP issues ZAP, Burp, SAST/DAST
Accessibility WCAG compliance axe-core, Lighthouse, manual keyboard testing
Chaos Does it degrade gracefully when a dependency fails? Kill a pod, add latency, drop the cache
Disaster recovery Can we actually restore? A scheduled restore drill 
// k6 — a load test with an SLO assertion, so it's a gate not a report
export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: '2m', target: 100 },   // ramp
    { duration: '5m', target: 100 },   // sustain
    { duration: '2m', target: 0 },     // ramp down
  ],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<300', 'p(99)<800'],
    http_req_failed:   ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

The most valuable question a stress test answers is not "what's the maximum throughput?" but "what does it look like when we exceed it?" Graceful degradation (429s, shed load, queue) or cascading collapse (timeouts, retry storms, OOM)? You want to discover that in a test, not at 09:00 on results day.

11. Legacy code

Michael Feathers' definition: legacy code is code without tests. The dependency problem is that you can't test it because it's coupled, and you can't safely decouple it because it's untested.

The way in:

  1. Characterisation tests — write tests that assert current behaviour, whatever it is. You're not judging correctness; you're building a safety net.
  2. Find a seam — a place where behaviour can be changed without editing the code in place (a virtual method, an interface, a parameter, a factory).
  3. Sprout method / sprout class — put new logic in a new, tested unit and call it from the old code, rather than adding to the mess.
  4. Wrap method — rename the old method and create a new one with the original name that calls it plus the new behaviour.
  5. Extract and test — pull a cohesive chunk into a testable unit, one small commit at a time.

Rule: don't refactor untested code and change behaviour in the same commit. Ever.

12. Checklist & interview angles

Test suite health checklist

  • Unit suite runs in under a minute locally
  • Full PR pipeline under ~10 minutes
  • Zero known-flaky tests in the blocking path
  • Tests run in parallel and in any order
  • No Thread.Sleep, no real network, no real clock
  • Names state behaviour; a failure is diagnosable from the name
  • Assertions on outcomes, not on interactions with mocks
  • Integration tests use real infrastructure (Testcontainers), not in-memory fakes
  • Every bug fix ships with a regression test
  • Coverage tracked as a delta, not a blanket target; mutation testing on critical modules
  • E2E limited to critical journeys, stable, and running on every merge
  • Load/security/accessibility tests scheduled and gating where appropriate

🔍 Interview angles

  • Pyramid or trophy? Both are heuristics; put the tests where the risk is. State that integration tests catch more in a CRUD/service-heavy system, and unit tests dominate where there's rich domain logic.
  • What makes a test bad? Slow, order-dependent, non-deterministic, asserting implementation details, or containing logic that can be wrong the same way the code is.
  • Why not mock the database? Constraints, transactions, SQL translation, and concurrency semantics are exactly what you need to test; an in-memory fake makes tests pass that will fail in production.
  • Is 100% coverage a good goal? No — coverage measures execution, not verification. Target meaningful coverage of business logic, use coverage delta as the gate, and use mutation testing to check the assertions are real.
  • How do you handle flaky tests? Quarantine immediately, then fix or delete. A suite that's red half the time trains everyone to ignore red.
  • How do you test time-dependent behaviour? Inject TimeProvider/a clock abstraction and advance it — never sleep.
  • How do you start testing a large untested legacy system? Characterisation tests around the area you must change, find a seam, sprout new tested code, then extract incrementally — never a big-bang refactor.
  • What's your definition of done? Give the list in §9 — it's a strong signal of operational maturity.
